analysis.investment_thesis: Crizac is a capital-light, debt-free international student recruitment intermediary compounding revenue at 66% CAGR with 36% ROE and 48% ROCE — extraordinary financial metrics for a P/E of only 20.8x. Fisher's rule of paying up for genuine growth applies here: the PEG ratio is under 0.35, making this genuinely cheap if even half the historical growth rate is sustained.
key_strengths: Exceptional growth quality: revenue INR 111→849 Cr (2021-25), net profit INR 21→153 Cr, all at expanding margins (operating margin 21.2%)
Pristine balance sheet: zero debt, INR 89 Cr cash, OCF positive all 4 years, INR 188 Cr FCF in 2025 — asset-light model needs almost no capex (INR 1 Cr in 2025)
Valuation anomaly: P/E of 20.8x / Forward P/E 16x for a 64% earnings CAGR — PEG <0.35 implies market deeply undervalues the growth runway
key_risks: Regulatory guillotine: Canada and UK have aggressively tightened student visa caps in 2024-25 — these are likely Crizac's largest destination markets, threatening volume
Intermediary moat is thin: no proprietary technology, R&D, or switching costs; university recruitment relationships can be replicated by competitors or disintermediated
Other income distortion: INR 35-53 Cr annually inflates reported profits; strip it out and 2025 net profit was closer to INR 118 Cr — operating earnings quality needs monitoring
red_flags: Canada/UK student intake volumes fell sharply in 2024-25 — the lag effect on Crizac's next 1-2 years of revenue is not yet fully visible in reported numbers
79.94% promoter holding severely limits public float and creates governance concentration risk
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Crizac scores exceptionally well on my core growth metrics — 66% revenue CAGR, 36% ROE, 48% ROCE, and zero debt is a combination I rarely see. The business is genuinely capital-light: capex was INR 1 Cr in both 2022-23 and 2025, meaning the company converts nearly all earnings to free cash. At P/E 20.8x with Forward P/E of 16x, the market is pricing in significant growth deceleration, which creates an opportunity if the company continues even at 25-30% growth. Fisher's scuttlebutt instinct tells me this is a company executing well in a large and underpenetrated market of Indian students seeking overseas education.

The critical concern is structural, not operational: Crizac is entirely dependent on the immigration policies of foreign governments. Canada slashed international student permits by 35% in 2024 and the UK has tightened visa rules — these are Crizac's primary destination markets. This is not a moat concern but an existential demand risk that cannot be managed away. The business model is also an intermediary with low switching costs — it lacks the innovation engine Fisher prizes most. The 2024 capex spike of INR 119 Cr (likely acquisitions or infrastructure investment) followed by a return to INR 1 Cr capex in 2025 warrants transparency. I rate it a BUY on valuation grounds alone, but with eyes open: this is a great business facing a potential cyclical air pocket from regulatory headwinds in its key markets.
